summary: Rizel Scarlett addresses the problematic industry practice of marketing AI agents as human software engineers, framing this as lazy marketing that prioritized quick sales to VCs and executives over sustainable developer adoption. Companies leaned into anthropomorphism to justify expensive AI tools to executives already paying engineers $300,000–$500,000, claiming AI could replace them. While anthropomorphism is not inherently harmful (e.g., eBooks with page-turning sounds, electric cars with engine sounds), it becomes self-sabotaging when applied to AI because the black-box nature makes capabilities and limitations harder to grasp. Marketing AI as thinking, reasoning, or working independently misleads users, alienates developers—who are AI's power users (76% use or plan to use AI per a 2024 Stack Overflow survey)—by telling them to adopt the tool and that it will replace them, and sets unrealistic expectations given real limitations: non-sentience, historical data training, context misses, hallucinations, and non-deterministic output. Scarlett references a Wired article where 30% of game developers expressed negative sentiment despite 52% company adoption. She proposes an eight-principle framework: understand how it works (become 'customer zero,' learn AI fundamentals like LLMs, tokens, context management, tool calling, agentic loops), name tools thoughtfully (use nonhuman names, avoid 'AI Engineer,' prefer 'co-pilot,' 'agent,' 'assistant'; GitHub's 'Copilot' naming is praised for signaling assistance not replacement), focus on augmentation over replacement (agents help developers multitask and work in parallel), be transparent (open source, white papers, conferences prevent misinformation—she shares how people theorized Copilot 'steals code' when internals weren't public), emphasize developer control (customize LLMs, verbosity, debugging logs, API integrations; Code named Goose praised for open source and MCP server support), show don't tell (use videos, gifs, blogs, live demos—even failed ones are teaching moments; she demoed Copilot writing a tweet at a conference), encourage documentation (installation guides, prompt playbooks, data usage transparency), and foster open collaboration (GitHub discussions, Discord; cursor.directory cited as a community-driven prompt collection). She concludes that how we present AI shapes how the world sees it, urging the industry to move beyond the replacement narrative.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Rizel Scarlett introduces herself as a staff developer advocate focusing on open source and AI, formerly at GitHub working on Copilot. She frames the talk as doing better developer marketing for AI agents through thoughtful anthropomorphism.

sections.title: Will AI Replace Software Engineers?
sections.summary: Discusses reactions to the 'will AI replace engineers' question—from eye-rollers to panickers. Notes companies like Salesforce making hiring decisions based on AI productivity (30% boost). Her stance: upskill and adapt, but internally wrestles with why AI is framed as replacement.

sections.title: The Spicy Take: Lazy Marketing and Anthropomorphism
sections.summary: Argues the industry shaped the replacement narrative through lazy marketing prioritizing quick wins over sustainable adoption. Companies leaned into anthropomorphism to sell tools to executives by claiming cost savings through engineer replacement. Defines anthropomorphism and gives benign examples (eBooks, electric cars).

sections.title: The Problem: Self-Sabotage and Alienating Developers
sections.summary: Explains why anthropomorphic AI marketing is self-sabotage: it misleads users, alienates developers (76% use AI per Stack Overflow survey), sets unrealistic expectations given AI limitations, and misses the real value of augmentation. Cites Wired article on game developers' negative sentiment toward AI.

sections.title: Framework for Thoughtful Anthropomorphism
sections.summary: Introduces eight-principle framework: understand how it works, thoughtfully name tools, focus on augmentation over replacement, be transparent, emphasize developer control, show don't tell, encourage clear documentation, foster open collaboration. Elaborates on understanding how tools work—become customer zero, learn AI fundamentals, understand agentic loops. Demonstrates with a test-generation agentic loop and a tic-tac-toe game with the 'Goose' AI agent.

sections.title: Thoughtful Naming and Augmentation Over Replacement
sections.summary: Concludes the tic-tac-toe demo noting the AI agent struggled with screen capture and lost the game, showing imperfection. Discusses thoughtful naming: use anthropomorphism sparingly, choose nonhuman names, avoid 'AI Engineer' titles, prefer 'co-pilot,' 'agent,' 'assistant.' Praises GitHub's 'Copilot' naming for signaling that the tool helps rather than replaces the developer. Discusses augmentation over replacement, referencing her blog post 'the average developer is a multitasker'—agents help developers work in parallel given their multiple roles.

sections.title: Transparency and Developer Control
sections.summary: Emphasizes transparency through open source, white papers, and conference talks to prevent misinformation. Shares a story about GitHub Copilot's beta period when people theorized on Twitter that it 'steals code' from repos, highlighting the need to get ahead of narratives before communities create false ones. Discusses developer control as trust-building: let users customize LLM choice, verbosity, debugging logs, and API integrations. Praises Code named Goose for being open source and connecting to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for extensibility.

sections.title: Show Don't Tell, Documentation, and Open Collaboration
sections.summary: Advocates showing rather than telling—use short videos, gifs, blogs, and live demos to demonstrate concrete capabilities like test creation, code conversion, wireframe-to-UI, and comment generation. Encourages live demos despite imperfection as teaching moments showing real troubleshooting. Shares a memorable GitHub Copilot demo where she wrote a tweet at a conference, generating audience excitement. Discusses documentation (installation guides, prompt playbooks, data usage transparency) and fostering open collaboration through GitHub discussions and Discord. Cites cursor.directory as a community-driven prompt collection. Recaps the full framework and closes by urging the industry to move beyond the AI-replaces-developers narrative.
